calls.reason: The CODA benchmark shows detectors struggle with corner cases, but no evidence ranks outliers above other barriers. Waymo's blog and a testing survey point to wider challenges, so whether outliers were the core issue is unsettled.

In June 2022, NHTSA's filing describes Tesla's systems as Level 2 needing driver supervision. Waymo's own blog shows driverless service only in parts of Phoenix plus employee-only rides in SF, far from anywhere-anytime use.

This is an undated long-run forecast. IIHS and Waymo studies show fewer crashes but no proven drop in deaths, and the AFB survey reports cost and accessibility barriers rather than lasting independence gains.

An IIHS survey found the Autopilot name led more people to think unsafe behavior was fine, and California's DMV ruled the branding misleading. NTSB tied a fatal crash partly to overreliance, which fits the risk Marcus described.

More than four years on, no Level 5 deployment turned up. A robotics professor said in October 2026 that Level 5 vehicles do not exist and will not for a decade, which fits any fair reading of 'any time soon'.

This is an open-ended claim that full self-driving needs an outlier solution. IIHS says only that Level 5 does not yet exist, which neither confirms that necessity nor shows whether the outlier problem has been solved.
